problem_framing.reason: A1 separates the objective (whether evidence justifies investment) from the suggested solution. It lists real alternatives: no expansion, a route-to-market change and redesign. It also names constraints on B2B relationships and reach to individual buyers. It does not reach rung 3. It misses that the dossier already shows a consumer-facing product (hlb-junior, found in A2), which bears on the 'beyond existing offering' premise. It also lists construction as a consumer use case. The €20,000 budget and 12-week window are not in the case and are framing assumptions only.

causal_mechanism.reason: T1 (A9) names who benefits and why behaviour changes (hearing protection seen as a fashion item or status symbol). It also names how value is captured (premium prices, specialty or direct-to-consumer channels, repeat purchase). The chain is asserted rather than grounded. The 'status symbol' step is slogan-like. Value capture ignores that Hellberg's demonstrated channels are B2B, so the full chain to value this manufacturer captures is not credibly traced.

distinct_theories.reason: T1 (lifestyle accessory, design-led, specialty or direct-to-consumer channels) and T2 (health or medical necessity, certification-led, medical supply channels, hearing-sensitive segment) imply different products, customers and channels. There is no 'no viable consumer demand' rival, but the rung 3 conditions are met.

assumptions_predictions.reason: The predictions are observable: a willingness-to-pay premium of at least 20% or 15%, higher purchase intent, and higher repeat purchase rate. The thresholds are arbitrary assumptions. T2's 'certified to medical standards' is vague. It is unclear that a modest stated-WTP shortfall would put either theory in real trouble, so rung 3 is not met.

evidence_judgement.reason: Each source gets a class label and a 'does not show' note, but key readings are wrong. A12 claims the hlb-junior product description 'indicates a medical necessity for children', which the text does not say. A14 labels bogoch-2005 as supporting T2 while admitting it does not show medical-necessity perception. A14 also misstates the finding: lack of concern about appearance becomes 'perceived as non-apparent', and an association under free provision becomes 'willingness increases when provided for free'. Crutzen-2021 (an intervention effect on earplug use) and en352-harmonised (no presumption of conformity under Regulation 2016/425, relevant to certification assumptions) were retrieved but never assessed.

seeking_challenge.reason: A13 searches against T1 but never assesses the results against T1. They are assigned only to T2 (A14, A15). Long-2024 is directly relevant to T1: nonusers mostly never considered hearing protection or worry about music quality, which is not a design or status motive. Bogoch's appearance-concern finding also bears on T1. The search did not reach the favoured theory and nothing found was reported against it.

experiment_design.reason: A randomized framing WTP survey could in principle separate lifestyle from medical framing. The decision rule in A17 is incoherent, though: '≥20% higher' is sufficient, '≥15% higher' is called 'within threshold', and 'less than threshold' means neither. T2 concerns a hearing-sensitive segment, but the sample is general adults, so the test does not address T2's stated customer. Stated WTP is not purchase behaviour. The cost and sample are assumptions.

revision.reason: No update was scheduled, and revision is excluded from packet.applicable_dimensions.

recommendation.reason: A19 recommends investing in a lifestyle proposition and rates T1 'likely'. The only T1 assessment (A11) is neutral, and the challenge evidence was never weighed against T1, so the position is unsupported. The next action conflates the test budget with a decision threshold: 'exceeds the €20,000 threshold'. Reversal conditions are stated, but the commitment to invest precedes the evidence that would justify it.

red_flags.reason: The hlb-junior description (children, school, concerts, lawn mowing) is read as indicating 'medical necessity'. The source does not say this.

Bogoch-2005 is scored as supporting T2 although the assessment itself says it does not show medical-necessity perception. Its finding is also misparaphrased as a free-provision effect and a non-apparent product.
T1 is rated 'likely' and investment is recommended with no supporting evidence. The only T1 assessment (A11) is neutral, and the challenge results (A13) were never applied to T1.
The test's decision rule is internally contradictory (the 20% and 15% thresholds overlap). The sample does not match T2's hearing-sensitive segment.
The next action confuses the €20,000 test budget with a willingness-to-pay difference threshold, which is a nonsensical decision criterion.
Relevant retrieved evidence was ignored: crutzen-2021 (intervention effect on use), en352-harmonised (certification and conformity limits) and long-2024 as a challenge to T1.
